claims.text: Service-relevant thermal exposure triggers decomposition of the initial non-equilibrium solid solution.
The solid-solution decomposition is diffusion controlled.
Thermal exposure causes Mg-rich intermetallic compounds to nucleate and grow.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds disrupt the continuity of the protective passive oxide film.
A continuous passive oxide film is responsible for the alloy's initially superior corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements.
The initial alloy has a continuous passive film.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds form both along grain boundaries and within grains.
Thermally activated diffusion promotes segregation of Mg and other alloying elements.
Elemental segregation leads to precipitation of discrete intermetallic phases.
Increasing intermetallic volume fraction and coarsening impair formation or maintenance of a coherent passive oxide film.
Loss of oxide-film coherence reduces corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Longer thermal exposures produce a higher volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds than the as-processed state.
Longer thermal exposures produce coarser Mg-rich intermetallic compounds than the as-processed state.
Intermetallic formation and coarsening coincide with a patchier passive oxide layer and degraded corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Shorter thermal treatments may produce a finer intermetallic dispersion that partially preserves passivation.
Temperatures of roughly 500–700 °C can provide sufficient thermal activation for diffusion in the intended service regime.
The proposed 500–700 °C regime is below that required to drive complete equilibrium transformation of the microstructure.
